title: The Sensor That Stopped: A Channel That Says What It Knows

questions.question: A driver calibrates, filters over 16 samples, and then rejects readings outside 0 to 30 m. A dropout reports zero counts. What happens?
options: Nothing is ever rejected, and sixteen outputs carry the bad reading
The dropout is rejected, as intended
The dropout is rejected one sample late
The filter removes it, so the check is unnecessary
questions.explanation: Calibrated the dropout is -0.43 m, which any check catches. Averaged with fifteen good readings of 5 m it is 4.66 m, which is an ordinary distance. The filter made it plausible before the check could see it.

questions.question: Does it matter whether you calibrate before filtering or after?
options: Mathematically no, they differ by 1.8e-15, but calibrate first so the range check is in metres
Yes, calibrating first is significantly more accurate
Yes, filtering first is significantly more accurate
No, and the order of the range check does not matter either
questions.explanation: A straight line through an average is the average of a straight line. The order that is forced is the check, and it is forced by measurement rather than by algebra.

questions.question: A device freezes and its driver keeps returning the last value. Your staleness check uses a timestamp taken when the reading reaches your code. What does it report?
options: ok, for ever: freshness computed from a stamp you wrote yourself is a statement about your own liveness
stale, one sampling period later
stale, once the buffer empties
stuck, since the value stops changing
questions.explanation: The channel stamped with the device's own time went stale one period after the freeze. The one stamped on arrival stayed ok for the whole run.

questions.question: You add a stuck detector that fires after five identical readings. On which sensor does it report a healthy parked device as stuck?
options: One whose noise is below its resolution: it then repeats for ever while working perfectly
Any sensor, if the robot is stationary long enough
One with high noise, where repeats are common
None, five is a safe threshold
questions.explanation: Measured over 100000 parked samples: at 50 times the resolution the longest natural run was 3, at equal to it 11, and at a tenth of it the sensor repeated for all 100000. The threshold has to come from the sensor.

questions.question: Your channel carries a filtered reading stamped at the moment its newest sample was taken. Why is carrying it forward by that age not enough?
options: An average is centred half a window earlier than its newest sample, so the filter's lag has to be added to the transport's
The timestamp is wrong and should be the moment of the oldest sample
Carrying forward cannot correct a filtered value at all
It is enough, since the filter adds no delay
questions.explanation: Measured end to end: carried forward by its age, 0.0199 m; carried forward by the lag the channel reports, 0.0123 m. Only the channel knows both halves.

questions.question: What does a driver owe its caller besides the number?
options: Whether the reading can be trusted, when it was taken, and how much lag it added
The raw counts alongside the calibrated value
The sensor's datasheet accuracy figure
Nothing else, if the number is correct
questions.explanation: A driver that returns a bare number forces every caller to guess at the difference between ok, stale, stuck and no data, and they guess ok. The lag matters because the loop downstream is spending from a budget.
